hints: Focus on solubility first, adding calcium ions can only cause a precipitate if it forms an insoluble calcium salt.
Remember that all nitrates, all chlorides except silver and lead, and all ammonium salts are soluble, so three of the options cannot precipitate.
Consider how hydroxide ions turn soluble $\text{HCO}_3^-$ into more $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$, which then joins with $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ to form an insoluble solid.
walkthrough:
**List what calcium could form**

Adding $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ adds $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{OH}^-$ to water that already has $\text{NH}_4^+$, $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$, $\text{HCO}_3^-$, $\text{Cl}^-$ and $\text{NO}_3^-$. A precipitate must be an insoluble combination.

Possible calcium solids:
$$\text{Ca}^{2+} + 2\text{Cl}^- , \text{Ca}^{2+} + 2\text{NO}_3^- , \text{Ca}^{2+} + \text{CO}_3^{2-}$$

**Apply solubility rules**

You know this lovely pattern well. All Group 1 and ammonium salts are soluble. All nitrates are soluble. Most chlorides are soluble.

That means $\text{CaCl}_2$, $\text{Ca(NO}_3)_2$ and any ammonium compound like $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ stay dissolved as ions.

**Spot the insoluble carbonate**

Calcium carbonate is famously insoluble. It is limestone, chalk and marble.

Precipitation reaction:
$$\text{Ca}^{2+}(aq) + \text{CO}_3^{2-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{CaCO}_3(s)$$

**See why hydroxide helps make even more**

The $\text{OH}^-$ does extra helpful work. It converts soluble hydrogencarbonate into carbonate.

$$\text{HCO}_3^-(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{CO}_3^{2-}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$
That new $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ then precipitates with $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ as well, so calcium carbonate is the solid removed.

options.A: Incorrect. $\text{CaCl}_2$ is very soluble in water. All chlorides are soluble except $\text{AgCl}$, $\text{PbCl}_2$ and $\text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2$, so no precipitate forms with $\text{Cl}^-$.
options.B: Correct. $\text{CaCO}_3$ is insoluble and precipitates. The added $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ reacts with the $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ already present, and the added $\text{OH}^-$ converts $\text{HCO}_3^-$ to extra $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ for even more precipitation.
options.C: Incorrect. $\text{Ca(NO}_3)_2$ is soluble in water. All nitrates are soluble with no exceptions, so $\text{NO}_3^-$ always stays in solution.
options.D: Incorrect. $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ does not exist as a precipitate. All ammonium salts are soluble, and ammonium hydroxide is fully miscible, existing as $\text{NH}_3(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. Hydroxide will actually release $\text{NH}_3$ gas, not a solid.
